cells.title: Understand the problem and the design tree
cells.task:
First, understand what the item's `background` asks for, just enough to know where to look in the design tree. Then
read the tree for this work, as the tree's rules say. Hand in `tree_entries`: every entry of the tree that bears on the
item. Read nothing else the `background` names in this run.

watches.name: background
watches.do: Look at what changed since the version you last worked from (all of it, if you have worked from none), read what the change touches, and hand in `tree_entries` as it now stands.

cells.title: Initial research
cells.task:
Research how to do what the item asks. Read the design tree as its rules say, beyond `tree_entries`, for what the
research reaches. Where the plan reaches entries that `tree_entries` does not name, hand in `tree_entries` again, the
whole list. Check that what the item says is true, where it can be seen. For a fault it reports, see the fault happen
where it really shows, such as in the program on its own data, and find its root cause. A cause read from the code, or a
test in a stand-in, such as a mock or a simulation of where it shows, has not seen it. For something it asks for, check
that it is not there already. If it is still not true after looking as far as the tools reach, ask the owner how to go
on, in a question that waits. Commit a test with the project's tests, and anything else you make in
`project.research`. If the design itself is at fault, say so.

Decide `deep_needed`. If it is yes, hand it in with `found` alone as soon as you see it, and research no further. If no,
write the plan (`plan_owner`, `plan_agent` and `acceptance`) and no `found`. Research every approach that could work.
When the design tree's rules say a choice is the owner's, ask about it in a question of its own: what to do, with each
approach as an option and what it gains and costs. If the solution conflicts with the design tree, ask instead of
bending the solution. Before handing in, ask yourself where the plan is most likely wrong, and check that point.

cells.title: Is there a better way
cells.task:
Think it through again from first principles. What does what `background` asks for really need, and does the plan
make sense for it? Is there a better way: the same result reached another way, more simply, with lower running cost or
less to maintain, with a better structure in the code, more complete in what it should cover, or truer to the
project's intent? Include ways that a decision of the tree rules out. Think again seriously; do not answer just to
have an answer.

If there is a better way, hand in `better_found`: what it is and why it is better, in a few sentences, without
repeating what the plan already says. If not, write no `better_found`.

watches.name: plan
watches.do: Think the plan through.

cells.title: Deep research
cells.task:
Research what `found` left open, and work out how to do what `background` asks. Read the design tree as its rules say,
beyond `tree_entries`, for what the research reaches, and read the code yourself. Where the plan reaches entries that
`tree_entries` does not name, hand in `tree_entries` again, the whole list. Treat `found` as a hypothesis to check. Use
what the research left in `project.research` instead of running it again, and commit anything you make there. Find
out the facts left open, try the approaches worth trying, and analyse a fault in the design itself as a design
problem. Check any fact that would change the direction before you rely on it, and weigh the upkeep the solution adds.

Write the plan: `plan_owner`, `plan_agent` and `acceptance`. In `plan_owner` say also what it leaves out. When the
design tree's rules say a choice is the owner's, ask about it in a question of its own, even where an experiment
favours one approach: what to do, with each approach as an option and what it gains and costs. If the solution
conflicts with the design tree, ask instead of bending the solution. Settle the rest from the facts, or decide it.

If the solution is too large for one work and splits into parts that can each be merged on their own, ask the
owner in a question that waits, listing the parts in order.

cells.title: Design review
cells.task:
You review the plan in a session of your own. You did not write it, so look for what its writer cannot see. Read the
code the plan changes. The plan is `plan_owner`, `plan_agent` and `acceptance`,
with the questions its writer asked the owner.

Judge it only by what it was made for (what `background` asks) and by the repository's rules, on each of these points:
1. Whether it does what `background` asks, no less and no more, and, if there was deep research, whether it settles
   what `found` left to it.
2. Its design, by the engineering rules: the responsibilities, interfaces and representations it touches, one place
   for each thing, and nothing that no current work needs.
3. The acceptance: whether each condition can be decided, whether a wrong result would fail it, and whether together
   they cover what `background` asks.
4. The questions: a question that a fact could settle; a choice the design tree's rules say is the owner's that no
   question asks; a question not marked in `plan_owner`; a question marked wrongly, `tree` yes for a choice that is not
   the owner's by the tree's rules, or no for one that is.

In the why of `plan_ok`, answer each point by its number: none, or what you found. Write everything the writer must deal
with in `plan_review`, all at once. If `plan_ok` is yes, leave `plan_review` out of your return. Leave out anything you
are not sure is better.

watches.name: plan
watches.do: Look at what changed in the plan since the version you last reviewed (all of it, if you have reviewed none), and review it.

watches.name: plan_review
watches.do: Where the writer answered an earlier point in `plan_review`, accept the answer or say why not. Never raise a point again without saying so, and raise nothing new that the answers did not bring up.

cells.title: Design tree review
cells.task:
You review the plan against the design tree, in a session that did not write it. Read the design tree as its rules
say, beyond `tree_entries`, for each part of the plan it leaves out, and read the code the plan changes. The plan is
`plan_owner`, `plan_agent` and `acceptance`, with the questions its writer asked the owner.

Judge whether the plan goes against the design tree: an article of the constitution, a principle or a decision.
Going against an entry is no fault where a question asks the owner about that change.

In the why of `tree_ok`, say what you found, or none. Write everything the writer must deal with in `tree_review`, all
at once. If `tree_ok` is yes, leave `tree_review` out of your return. Leave out anything you are not sure of.

watches.name: plan
watches.do: Look at what changed in the plan since the version you last reviewed (all of it, if you have reviewed none), and review it.

watches.name: tree_review
watches.do: Where the writer answered an earlier point in `tree_review`, accept the answer or say why not. Never raise a point again without saying so, and raise nothing new that the answers did not bring up.

cells.title: Implement
cells.task:
Implement `plan_agent`, changing only what this work needs. Read the design tree as its rules say, beyond
`tree_entries`, for what the change touches. For each question put to the owner, follow the option the
owner took, or else the one it recommends. For each answered question marked `tree`, write the option taken into the
design tree, as its rules say. If main's tree has changed since, an entry may follow its wording and place, but not
change its meaning. After you change the tree, run `project.tree_check` and fix what it
finds before you run your tests.

Where a test can show what the change is for, start from one that is red on the code before the change: use the
research's test where it left one. Run each test you add or extend both on the change and on the code before it. A test
that you remove, skip or weaken needs a technical reason. Where the cost per operation or request can change, measure
what could get slower as well as what the change is for.

If the plan does not hold (its direction is wrong, or it needs a decision of the tree changed, or a choice the owner
has not made, such as accepting a slowdown), do not work around it. Say where and why in `plan_doubts`. The answer
comes there too: judge it, and write `plan_doubts` again only where a doubt still stands.

Commit everything in the worktree, and hand in `code`, `decisions` and `evidence` once what you ran through
`run_tests` for the change passes on your last commit. Hand in `title` with your first `code`, and again when what the
change does changes; `decisions` only where there is one; and `acceptance` only when a condition must change, as the
whole list as it now stands, with why.

If main does not merge into the branch, merge it in yourself and run the check again. Fix a point its judge insists
on, or have the owner rule on it. If what the item asks needs no change, ask the owner.

cells.title: Code review
cells.task:
Review the code of the change in `code`, in a session of your own, and change no files. Read the diff from main to
`head`. Judge only by what the implementation was asked to do (`plan_owner`, `acceptance`) and by the repository's
rules. Old code that already lagged behind a decision before this work is not a point. Do not review the tests or the
design tree.

1. Does the code do what the plan says, with no shortcut, different method, change of direction, or more than the work
   needs?
2. Is it well built, by the standards of software engineering?
3. Does the change reach every place where the same thing happens, not only the one the item names?
4. Does each decision in `decisions`, and each one the code makes that `decisions` does not list, rest on a reason that
   holds?
5. Is each exception or expected value that the change gives a check a deliberate design choice, not a fault it hides?
6. Is each change to a file the project protects one the work needs?

In the why of `review_ok`, answer each question by its number: what you checked and what you found. A question you did
not check is a point: say what must be shown. Write every point in `review` at once. Leave out preferences: the engineer
fixes nearly everything a review raises, so a wrong point makes good code worse. If `review_ok` is yes, leave `review`
out of your return.

watches.name: change
watches.do: Look at what changed since the version you last reviewed (all of it, if you have reviewed none), and review it.

watches.name: review
watches.do: Look at what changed: accept each answer in `review` or say why not, and raise nothing new that the fix did not bring up.

cells.title: Test review
cells.task:
Review the tests and the evidence of the change in `code`, in a session of your own, and change no files. Read the
diff from main to `head`. Judge only by what the implementation was asked to do (`plan_agent`, `acceptance`) and by the
repository's rules. Do not review the code or the design tree.

1. Does `evidence` show each condition of `acceptance` on the change?
2. Was each new or extended test red on the code before the change, where its kind needs that, as a run shows?
3. For each test the change removes, skips, narrows or weakens: is what it checked still checked, or is a technical
   reason given?
4. Is each new test worth its time: what does it catch that no other test does, and why can it not be smaller?
5. Where the cost per operation or request can change, is what could get slower measured?
6. Does the change touch a kind that `needs_testing` names?

In the why of `test_ok`, answer each question by its number: what you checked and what you found. In the why of
`needs_testing`, give the kind the change touches, or say that it touches none. A question you did not check is a point:
say what must be shown. Write every point in `test_review` at once. Leave out preferences: the engineer fixes nearly
everything a review raises, so a wrong point makes good code worse. If `test_ok` is yes, leave `test_review` out of your
return. Once you have said yes to `needs_testing`, keep it while the part of the change that made you say so is still
there.

watches.name: change
watches.do: Look at what changed since the version you last reviewed (all of it, if you have reviewed none), and review it.

watches.name: test_review
watches.do: Look at what changed: accept each answer in `test_review` or say why not, and raise nothing new that the fix did not bring up.

cells.title: Design tree review of the change
cells.task:
Review the change in `code` against the design tree, in a session of your own, and change no files. Read the diff from
main to `head`, and read in full each file of decisions whose topic the change touches. Judge the code and the tests
only for these questions.

1. Does the change go against a principle or a decision of the tree, where no question asked the owner about that
   change?
2. Is the option taken in each question marked `tree` written into the tree, and does every other change of the tree
   mend an entry the change made untrue?
3. Did the work make a choice that the tree's rules give the owner, in the plan, in `decisions` or in the code, that no
   question put to him?
4. Does the change leave an entry of the tree untrue, or a comment that goes against the tree?

In the why of `design_ok`, answer each question by its number: what you checked and what you found. A question you did
not check is a point: say what must be shown. Write every point in `design_review` at once. Leave out preferences: the
engineer fixes nearly everything a review raises, so a wrong point makes good code worse. If `design_ok` is yes, leave
`design_review` out of your return.

watches.name: change
watches.do: Look at what changed since the version you last reviewed (all of it, if you have reviewed none), and review it.

watches.name: design_review
watches.do: Look at what changed: accept each answer in `design_review` or say why not, and raise nothing new that the fix did not bring up.

cells.title: Adversarial testing
cells.task:
Test the change in `code` in a session of your own, and look for where it is wrong. You only write tests, in the
project's test files. Where you think the implementation is wrong, write a test that turns red, for the engineer to
fix. For each condition of `acceptance` that a test can show, make sure a test shows it: the engineer's test where it
really tests the condition, otherwise one of yours. Then dig for corner cases. Each of your tests names the
independent reference its verdict rests on, such as a specification or an established implementation. What you think
should hold does not count. A test of new behaviour fails before the change; a test of old behaviour passes before and
after it. Run every test that is new in this work, both on the change and on the code before it. If one of your tests
gives a result before the change that does not fit its kind, fix it and run it again now. If one of the engineer's
tests does, say so in `testing`. If a test is red after the change, check it against its reference first, and hand on
only what stays red. Commit your tests on the work's branch.

Hand in `tests`, and write what stays red or suspect in `testing`, every point at once. If `testing_ok` is yes, leave
`testing` out of your return.

watches.name: testing
watches.do: Run your tests on the new commit. Accept each answer in `testing` or say why not, and check any test that an answer calls wrong against its reference.

blocks.name: head
